content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper claims that exsisting KD methods can't work well between attention and convolution based networks. To this end, this paper proposes a encoder-decoder style distiilation method via PCA to help CNN architectures learns from Swin-Transformer teacher.   Specifically, the authors argue that the intermediate outputs of the student network (CNN) can be decomposed into latent variables with global information through PCA decomposition. With a linear projection we can aligen such global information with teacher network (ViT).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
- To the best of my knowledge, this work is the first to discussion distill ViT to CNN, and the idea is reasonable.
- The experimental results of this paper appear to be sufficient and great.

# Weakness
I have concerns about this paper in theory, methodology, and experiments.
## Theory
- The paper proposes information bottleneck theory at the beginning, which looks interesting but does not directly prove the relationship between the proposed method and IB theory (if it does, please point it out).
- All the lemmas are too obvious that the given proofs are like homework in a graduate program. 
## Methodology
- This paper mentions that the complexity of self-attention is $O(n^2d)$, which seems very high. But the computational complexity of PCA itself can be higher than self-attention ($O(n^3) $ for 1 of $d$ channel). The complexity of this paper is much larger than related works.
- PCA's output is not unique due to multiple direction of sigular vectors and multiple root of eigenvalue. And the linear projection $W_2$ should also be optimzied for every aligned embedding of every single sample in every single step. 
## Experiments
- This paper mentioned multiple combination of fancy tricks, including warmup,  cosine decay learning strategy,  and advanced augmentations "such as" three methods without any corrosponding hyper-parameters. If "such as" means they are just part of all augmentations? I am concerned about the reproducibility of the experiments.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is well written and easy to follow. But the math proof seems not enough to cover all of author's claim.

Novelty: This task is quite interesting, while the method dosen't appeal to me.

Reproducibility: This paper provide insufficient details to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I have concerns about the theory, methodology and experiments of this paper.
In theory, I am concerned that the paper does not demonstrate the core motivation (Information Bottleneck). The so-called proof makes no theoretical contribution.
In methodology, the optimization process looks very cumbersome and has extremely high training complexity.
In experments, detail is not sufficient enough, no provided traning log or any benchmark. Reproducibility is questionable.

All in all, my recommendation is rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work presents a new distillation method by teaching CNNs with (Swin) transformer. The final layer representation of a transformer network is projected to low rank space via PCA within a mini batch. Such low rank feature is applied to guide learning of student network. Marginal performance improvements are observed on ImageNet1k and ImageNet100.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The writing of this work is generally clear. The entire method is well presented in a mathematical language. Some theoretical analyses are built around the proposed approach, which may add value and provide insight.

On the other hand, the introduction section is not sufficient to justify why distilling knowledge from transformer to CNN is a preferred framework versus transformer to transformer, CNN-CNN or others within the same architecture category. Empirically, the authors also ignore the comparison with other CNN-CNN and transformer-transformer distillation methods. This is the top priority to consolidate the motivation of this work.

Table 1 shows that LRRA only improves less than 1% across all discussed CNN models while being much less than the original gap (>10%) between Swin and CNN. This experiment result weakens the contribution of this work actually and brings up my question above again. 

In addition, as the authors mention, the dimension of PCA feature is smaller than the number of data in a mini-batch. Consequently, the resulting PCA representation over a mini-batch is just an over-complete and possibly de-noised embedding. Projecting arbitrary mini-batch to a single low-rank subspace is fundamentally sub-optimal since data in generally resides in highly non-linear space after transformer.  So methodologically it is hard to understand why PCA is a good way to preserve global information and in turn why a single low-rank per mini-batch is a preferred way to distill knowledge. The first ablation study tries to answer this question but only shows marginal improvement (<0.5%) from a single MLP layer. What if we use a single attention layer or multi-MLP layers? I don't see any reason why a generic learning module cannot replace the functionality of PCA.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation is in good quality and the work seems to be easy to reproduce. The authors did not mention whether to share the code/experiment details in public.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work is lacking a solid ground in defending the necessity of distilling transformer for CNN and why it is a promising way of distillation. The experiment only shows marginal improvement, which further aggravates my concerns about its technical contribution. I am leaning towards the rejection

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The article proposes a method that enables knowledge transfer from the Transformer-base model to the CNN-base model. The method focuses on encoding (matrix decomposition) as well as decoding (approximate estimation) the features from the student model (CNN) to align them with the features from the teacher model (Transformer).

The most critical contribution is the provision of a new distillation method, a way to distill from the Transformer model into the CNN model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
1. The article proposes a new way to help CNN models improve their performance, by using Transformer models as teachers. (Prior to this, more distillation approaches were using models with the same architecture)
2. The proposed method and the ablation experiment help the reader understand how the method works and the adequate validation of each part.

Weaknesses
1. In METHODOLOGY, what is the relationship between the decoder loss in equation 10 and the dis loss in equation 12?
2. In METHODOLOGY, the first paragraph mentions that the method used in the article is mainly to select the output of the penultimate layer for distillation. This is a very interesting choice. The proposed method should also be applicable to feature distillation in the middle layer of the network, so why not choose a feature-base for distillation? In other words, what is the advantage of doing this over feature-based distillation?
3. In the proposed method, one of the key calculations is Singular Value Decomposition. The following article is based on the distillation of intermediate features output from the model, and also uses the Singular Value Decomposition. Perhaps some discussion is warranted?

Lee S H, Kim D H, Song B C. Self-supervised knowledge distillation using singular value decomposition[C]//Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV). 2018: 335-350.

4. In EXPERIMENTS, the authors specifically compare feature distillation methods with parameters, but in addition, we may also be concerned about computational speed (Flops), so it would be better to add a comparison?
5. There are many kinds of Transformer architectures, why do only take SwinTransformer for experiments?

Others
1. The articles motivation to distill CNN models from Transformer is not enough to attract. In fact, it is difficult for us to see the practical application value of this work. From the experimental results, we can find that the Transformer lead to limited performance improvement for CNN models. For distillation, the gap between models is critical, the design architecture gap between CNN and Transformer models is relatively large, and the experimental results are not attractive enough for us to use Transformer models to distill CNN models.
2. As far as the proposed method is concerned, is it also feasible for CNN models as teachers? This method does not reflect its advantages over the Transformer model
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The article is written in a way that clearly describes how the method works, is logically self-consistent and conducts sufficient experiments for validation. However, the motivation for writing is not clear enough.
content.summary_of_the_review: The article mainly wants to perform knowledge distillation on CNN models with Transformer models as teachers, and the paper proposes an interesting approach to perform knowledge alignment of the two architectural models. However, the practicality is limited in terms of experimental results; the design approach does not reflect the advantages of the Transformer model.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to distill ViTs' knowledge to CNNs, which is a new research direction that has not been explored yet. A Low Rank Representation Approximation (LRRA) approach, based on matrix decomposition and Encoder-Decoder architecture, is proposed to tackle this problem in a closed-form solution manner.  
A benchmark is introduced, where experiments are conducted on ImageNet-100 and 6 CNN models. The proposed approach achieved incremental improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. The ablation study is extensive, and the individual contribution of each component is demonstrated.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1: Clear motivation. This paper is well-motivated. Transferring knowledge from ViTs to CNNs is interesting. 

2: The paper is overall easy to follow/read.

3: Solid ablation study. Extensive experiments are conducted.

4: Theoretical support. 

Main weaknesses:

1: The improvements over other methods are quite incremental.

2: Though the motivation is to transfer ViT's knowledge to small-scale CNNs. It is still desirable to have larger CNN models to build a more comprehensive benchmark.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good clarity and presentation.

Quality: Solid in method/theory, but lack of sufficient experiments to demonstate the effectiveness of the proposed method. 

Novelty: Fair. 

Reproducibility: Training details are provided.

content.title: Distill Vision Transformers to CNNs via Low-Rank Representation Approximation
content.TL;DR: Distill Vision Transformers to CNNs via Low-Rank Representation Approximation
content.abstract: Vision Transformers attain state-of-the-art performance in diverse vision tasks due to their scalable and long-range dependencies modeling. Meanwhile, CNNs are still practical and efficient in many industry scenarios, thanks to their inductive biases and mature tiny architectures. Thus it is a challenging yet interesting problem to study the Knowledge Distillation (KD) of these two different architectures. In particular, how to transfer global information from Vision Transformers to tiny CNNs. We point out that many current CNN distillation methods are ineffective in the Vision Transformers distillation scenario, which implies that distilling global information is not easy due to the architecture gaps. We develop an encoder-decoder representation distillation framework, namely \textbf{L}ow \textbf{R}ank \textbf{R}epresentation \textbf{A}pproximation, to address the problem. The Key insight of LRRA is that the global information modeling can be seen as finding the most important bases and corresponding codes. This process can be solved by matrix decomposition. Specifically, the student representation is encoded to a low-rank latent representation and used to approximate the teacher representation. The most distinguishable knowledge, i.e., global information, is distilled via the low-rank representation approximation. The proposed method offers a potential closed-form solution without introducing extra learnable parameters and hand-crafted engineering. We benchmark 11 KD methods to demonstrate the usefulness of our approach. Extensive ablation studies validate the necessity of the low-rank structure.
